title: The Iranian Revolution of 1979

cards.h: A king is overthrown, a republic is born
cards.b:
In 1979 the Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, fled the country. Within months the monarchy was replaced by an Islamic Republic led by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini. The revolution changed Iran, the Middle East and Western policy for decades.

It is one of the most important events of the late twentieth century. Its causes are still debated, and its effects are still felt in the region.

The Shah ruled from 1941. In the early 1960s he launched the White Revolution, a programme of land reform, literacy drives and women's rights, paid for by oil revenue. Many of these changes were welcomed, but they also angered traditional clergy and the rural poor.

The Shah relied on SAVAK, a feared secret police, to crush opposition. Critics said he was a dictator who ignored the people, and his court grew rich and distant.

Khomeini had opposed the Shah since 1963 and was exiled in 1964. He lived in Turkey and Iraq, and from 1978 in France. From his exile he sent tapes and messages to Iran, and his speeches were copied and passed from hand to hand.

His lectures in Najaf in 1970 argued for rule by Islamic jurists, the doctrine called velayat-e faqih. This became central to the republic he built after 1979.

cards.h: Ervand Abrahamian, Iran Between Two Revolutions (1982)
cards.b:
Ervand Abrahamian (1982)

Abrahamian argues that the 1979 revolution was a coalition. Clerics, students, merchants, workers and leftist groups all took part, and each had its own goals. He looks at the social roots of the protests and at how leaders built alliances across these groups.

His book is a key counter to the view that the revolution was purely religious.
The Shah left Iran on 16 January 1979. Khomeini returned on 1 February. In April, a referendum set up the Islamic Republic.

On 8 September 1978, soldiers fired on a huge crowd in Jaleh Square in Tehran. Many people were killed, and the day became known as Black Friday. Strikes spread through oil fields, banks and government offices in the autumn.

The oil strikes hurt the state badly, because oil was its main source of income. By late 1978 the Shah's position was collapsing. His government fell to a wave of protest and desertion.

cards.h: Was it purely a religious revolution?
cards.b:
Many Western accounts describe the revolution as a religious uprising led by mullahs. The image of the veiled crowd and the clerical leader dominates the story.

Historians argue this view is too simple. Students, leftists, bazaar merchants and workers all played crucial roles. Khomeini was the leader who united them, but the revolution was not only a religious one. The later rule of the clergy narrowed its aims.

In November 1979 militant students stormed the US embassy in Tehran and took 52 Americans hostage. They were held for 444 days. The crisis dominated American politics, and it helped defeat President Jimmy Carter in 1980.

The hostages were released on 20 January 1981, just as Carter left office. The crisis showed how deeply the revolution had shaken the relationship between Iran and the United States.

cards.h: A republic built on clerical rule
cards.b:
The new constitution gave final authority to the leader, the supreme jurist, and created a Guardian Council to vet laws and candidates. Elections were held, but power lay with the clergy and with institutions they controlled.

Historians argue whether the system is a democracy with religious limits or a religious state with elections. The answer depends on how you define democracy, and Iranians themselves still debate it.

In September 1980 Iraq invaded Iran. The Iran-Iraq War lasted until 1988 and killed hundreds of thousands. The war helped the new regime consolidate power, and it made the revolution's leaders see themselves as defending the nation.

The war changed Iran's military and its foreign policy. It also left lasting debts and wounds on both sides.

In 1977 Indira Gandhi's Emergency, which had lasted since 1975, ended with her defeat in general elections. The Janata Party came to power in Delhi, a moment when democracy in India faced one of its hardest tests.

Two very different revolutions and regime changes were happening in the same decade. In India, voters removed a leader from power at the ballot box. In Iran, a monarchy fell to a mass movement and a new clerical state.

Five things to remember
  1. The Shah left Iran on 16 January 1979.
  2. Khomeini returned on 1 February 1979.
  3. Black Friday, 8 September 1978, was a turning point.
  4. The revolution was a coalition of groups.
  5. The US hostage crisis lasted 444 days.
Think about it
  • Can a revolution be both popular and authoritarian?
  • Did the revolution fail, or did it succeed in its own terms?
